ext.title: Influencing Connected Legislators
ext.venue: NBER Working Paper No. 22739 (October 2016; JEL D72, D78). Not peer-reviewed per the NBER disclaimer. Metadata hint confirmed: authors, year, and NBER w22739 are correct.
ext.document_type: NBER working paper (theory plus empirical estimation)
ext.coverage: Read all 3,019 lines of the text file (110,304 chars, under the 400,000 limit) in six chunks. Covered: front matter, abstract, Introduction (Sec 1), Model (Sec 2), Equilibrium contributions (Sec 3 incl. Lemma 1, Props 1-3), Evidence from the U.S. Congress (Sec 4 incl. data, controls, networks, Heckman/control-function correction, results), Discussion and extensions (Sec 5), Conclusions (Sec 6), References, Appendix proofs (Sec 7), and Tables 1-5 with notes. Not in the text file: Tables A.1-A.3 (data appendix), the online appendix (Lemma 3.1/3.2 proofs, Lemma 1 policy-motivated proof, Sec 5 threshold derivations), and any figure beyond the textual description of Figure 1. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this PDF (task specified none), so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: Do legislators' social ties affect how interest groups allocate campaign contributions? Specifically, how do interest groups allocate money across legislators connected by a social network, and do legislators' network positions (Bonacich centrality) predict PAC contributions in the U.S. House?
ext.theory: Two interest groups (one for policy A, one against) each have a budget and promise contingent payments to legislators, who vote after observing offers. Legislators value contributions (concave utility, log in the estimation), value conformity with their social network (weights G, so utility rises with peers voting the same way), and may care about the policy (policy motivation; office-motivated legislators have zero policy preference). Interest groups do not know legislators' preferences exactly (uniform noise with density Psi). Under Assumptions 1 (sufficient noise, Psi small) and 2 (I - beta*G invertible and positive), there is a unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (Props 1-2). With office-motivated legislators the equilibrium transfers maximize a weighted sum of legislators' monetary utilities with weights equal to Bonacich centralities (Prop 1, Sec 3.2.1). With policy-motivated legislators the weights are modified Bonacich centralities (eq. 15, Prop 2). As the number of legislators grows, or as policy preference weakens, the modified weights converge to simple Bonacich centralities (Corollary 1; Prop 3, Sec 3.2.2). The central empirical implication is that the network externality parameter (phi*) must be positive for social ties to matter.
ext.data: Unit: legislator-Congress observations for U.S. House members (stacked across Congresses). Sample periods: 109th-113th Congresses (election cycles 2004-2012). Each committee network has roughly 440 Representatives (including midterm replacements) and about 20 standing committees; the alumni network has over 400 nodes and thousands of links (fn. 11). Regression N: committee-network specification 2,128 observations; alumni-network specification 1,166 observations (more than 50% of congressmen linked by alma mater; Sec 4.2.1). Dependent variable: total PAC contributions to each candidate in $ millions, from FEC files aggregated by the Center for Responsive Politics, trimmed at 1st and 99th percentiles; range $9,519 to $7,178,406; total PAC spending $310 million (110th) to $453 million (112th) (Sec 4.2.2). Cosponsorship data for Table 1: all bills proposed in the House 109th-113th Congresses from THOMAS (244,519 dyads for alumni-cosponsorship; 242,735 dyads for committee-membership). Controls: margin of victory (FEC publications, supplemented by state agencies), per capita income by district (ACS one-year estimates), DW-NOMINATE first dimension (Nokken-Poole modified coordinates), committee chair, seniority, relevant powerful committee (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Appropriations, Rules, Financial Services), joint committee (Economic, Taxation, Library, Printing), party (Republican=1), gender, top-10 university attendance (about 6% of congressmen), four election-cycle dummies. Committee and roster data: Clerk of the House, Stewart and Woon site, CQ roster for the 113th; alumni: Biographical Directory of Congress; ideology/party/gender: GovTrack.
ext.method: Theory: backward induction over a two-stage game (voting stage then influence stage); existence by Brouwer; uniqueness via Lemma 1 (unique voting equilibrium when office-motivated, or policy-motivated with sufficient uncertainty); equilibrium characterized as maximization of weighted monetary utilities (Props 1-2). Empirical: a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model, s = alpha*1 + phi* W s + beta'X + eps (eq. 23), where s is log-transformed contribution-related outcome (eq. 17-18 derive log utility FOC; eq. 20-22 derive the SAR form), estimated by maximum likelihood (Anselin 1988). Benchmarks: OLS without network effects, AIC comparisons, likelihood-ratio test of phi*=0 (chi-square, 1 df), and OLS with degree, betweenness and closeness centrality (Table 4). Robustness: party-weighted committee network, chairmanship-weighted committee network, alumni networks with graduation-period windows (4 and 2 years). Multiple interest groups (Sec 5.2), threshold objectives (Sec 5.3) and heterogeneous policies (Sec 5.4) are extensions that leave the SAR form unchanged up to scale.
ext.identification: Committee network: links are proportional to shared committees, which may be endogenous to unobserved legislator traits that also drive contributions. The authors use a control-function (Heckman-style) correction following Qu and Lee (2015): a first-stage linear probability dyadic model of committee sharing on characteristic distances (eq. 24), then the first-stage residual term is added to the outcome equation (eq. 25). Exclusion: dyad-specific variables in link formation are excluded from the outcome equation; Table 2 column (2) reports the correction. The assumption that the selection effect is the same for all politicians is stated in fn. 23. Alumni network: asserted exogenous by construction to the political process, since shared institutions predate election; no selection correction is applied. Validity of the alumni network is argued via Table 1 panel (a) (alumni links predict cosponsorship) and panel (b) (alumni links barely predict committee sharing, R^2 0.002-0.003). Cosponsorship is not used to build the network because it is endogenous to contributions (fn. 30).
ext.scope: Population: U.S. House of Representatives members serving in the 109th through 113th Congresses (election cycles 2004-2012), with PAC contributions from FEC/CRP data. Institution: Congress with House committee structure and PAC campaign finance. Era: 2004-2012 cycles. Theory applies to any network with a finite number of legislator types. The authors note that the theory is about monetary transfers and social networks in legislatures generally. Not studied: Senate, state legislatures, non-monetary resources, lobbyist behavior, and endogenous changes in network topology.

key_findings.finding: Equilibrium exists and is unique in pure strategies under Assumption 1 (noise sufficiently large) and Assumption 2; with office-motivated legislators the optimal transfer allocation maximizes a weighted sum of monetary utilities with weights equal to Bonacich centralities. Under log utility the transfer is proportional to Bonacich centrality.
key_findings.numbers: Assumption 1: Psi*(beta_max + ...) <= 1/2 (bound on the noise density Psi); Assumption 2: I - 2*Psi*G invertible and positive. Proportionality factor depends on the shadow cost of money.

key_findings.finding: With policy-motivated legislators the allocation weights become modified Bonacich centralities that depend on preferences and pivot probabilities; they converge to simple Bonacich centralities as the policy-preference weight goes to zero and as the number of legislators grows large.
key_findings.location: Sec 3.2.2 (eq. 15-16, Prop 2, p. 15); Corollary 1 (p. 15-16); Prop 3 (p. 16); proof in Sec 7.3 (p. 39-40)
key_findings.numbers: Prop 3: convergence as n goes to infinity; the proof uses Lemma 3.2 (pivot probabilities and their derivatives go to zero).

key_findings.finding: Committee-network estimate of the network externality parameter is positive and significant; with the control-function correction it is slightly larger.
Alumni-network estimate of the externality parameter is positive and significant.
Network effects significantly improve model fit over OLS without network terms; the likelihood ratio test rejects phi = 0 in both networks.
key_findings.numbers: Committee: AIC OLS 5686.323 vs MLE 5679.196; LR statistic 11.127. Alumni: AIC OLS 3201.537 vs MLE 3193.922; LR statistic 9.615. Table brackets show p = 0.003 (committee) and p = 0.001 (alumni), while the text says p-value equal to 0.000.

key_findings.finding: Standard centrality measures (degree, closeness, betweenness) do not explain PAC contributions; the model with them fits no better than the no-network baseline.
key_findings.numbers: Degree 0.0004 (SE 0.0003) in committee network, -0.0018 (SE 0.0053) in alumni network; Closeness 0.5902 (SE 0.4711) and 0.5903 (SE 0.4771); Betweenness -4.9e-05* (SE 2.9e-05) in committee network, -3.2e-05 (SE 5e-05) in alumni; R^2 = 0.148 across all Table 4 specifications.

key_findings.finding: Results are robust to party-weighted and chairmanship-weighted committee networks and to alumni networks restricted to overlapping graduation periods. The party-weighted estimate is larger than baseline.
key_findings.numbers: Party-weighted committee network: phi = 0.2486*** (SE 0.0656) MLE; 0.2588*** corrected. Chairmanship-weighted: 0.3575*** (SE 0.0866) and 0.2152*** (corrected). Alumni, 4-year window: 0.07700*** (SE 0.0290), N = 767. Alumni, 2-year window: 0.06694** (SE 0.0306), N = 597.

key_findings.finding: Alumni links strongly predict cosponsorship but barely predict committee sharing, supporting the claim that the alumni network is a distinct channel from committee-based ties.
key_findings.numbers: Alumni link on cosponsorship: 0.180*** (SE 0.008) bare, 0.069*** (SE 0.007) with controls; R^2 rises from 0.008 to 0.11. Alumni link on committee membership: 0.006 (SE 0.006) bare, 0.012* (SE 0.007) with controls; R^2 0.002-0.003. Authors state the alumni network explains less than 1% of committee formation versus about 11% of endorsement.

key_findings.finding: Control coefficients have the signs the literature predicts: chairs and relevant-committee members get more PAC money; close races, ideological extremity and seniority are associated with lower or higher contributions as stated; Republicans receive more.
key_findings.numbers: Chair 0.4006*** (SE 0.0967) committee; Margin of Victory -0.8972*** (SE 0.0885); DW_ideology -1.0774*** (SE 0.1241); Party (Republican) 0.1443** (SE 0.0573); Per capita income 0.0061** (SE 0.0025).

limitations: Authors describe this as a first attempt to bring predictions to data; they note significant room for further analysis (Sec 6, p. 30-31).
Theory covers only monetary transfers; non-monetary resources (expertise, contacts) are left for future work (Sec 6).
Interest groups do not alter network topology in the model; linking that to Ballester, Calvo-Armengol and Zenou (2006) key-player analysis is left open (Sec 6).

Committee network may be endogenous; the control-function correction is parametric and assumes the selection effect is identical across legislators (fn. 23); the selection term's sign suggests unobserved expertise drives both contributions and network links (Sec 4.3).
Bootstrapped standard errors (1,000 replications) are used because no closed-form adjustment exists for the generated regressor (fn. 25).
Alumni sample (N = 1,166) oversamples top-10 university graduates; a top-10 dummy is included, and top-10 attendance is about 6% of congressmen (Sec 4.2.2).
Cosponsorship is not used as the network because it is itself an endogenous outcome (fn. 30).
Policy-motivated case requires sufficient uncertainty (Assumption 3 / Lemma 1); the proofs for policy-motivated legislators are in the online appendix, not the text file.
Modified Bonacich weights are laborious to compute for large networks and depend on preferences and the voting rule, not only topology (Sec 3.2.2, p. 15).
Closed-form Bonacich relation depends on utility specification (fn. 3); logarithmic utility is assumed for the empirical mapping (Sec 4.1).

Reviewer-level caveats from this extraction: the text layer garbles Greek symbols (phi*, beta, psi, Psi), so the exact formula defining the SAR parameter is reconstructed from surrounding text. The text states p = 0.000 for the LR tests but the table brackets show 0.003 and 0.001. The introduction says the outcome is business PAC contributions, while Sec 4.2.2 describes total PAC contributions. Table A.1 (variable definitions and summary statistics) is not in the text file.
measures: Bonacich centrality b(beta,G) = (I - beta*G)^{-1} * 1 (eq. 4), with decay parameter beta; modified Bonacich (eq. 15).
Dependent variable: total PAC contributions to each congressman, $ millions (trimmed at 1st/99th percentiles).
Committee network link: number of shared committees (count), with party-weighted and chairmanship-weighted variants.
Alumni network link: 1 if two members graduated from the same institution (undergraduate or graduate); variants require overlapping graduation periods of 4 or 2 years.
Degree centrality (count of direct links), betweenness centrality, closeness centrality (normalized by degree).

Control variables: margin of victory, per capita district income, DW-NOMINATE dimension 1, chair, seniority, relevant committee, joint committee, party, gender, top-10 university, election-cycle dummies.
Cosponsorship link counts (directional) from THOMAS for Table 1.
Fit measures: AIC, likelihood-ratio statistic (chi-square, 1 df), R^2 for OLS benchmarks.
references_of_note: Ballester, Calvo-Armengol and Zenou (2006), Econometrica: 'Who's who in networks. Wanted: the key player'. Basis for Bonacich-centrality policy and network-externality model.
Bonacich (1987), American Journal of Sociology: power and centrality family of measures. Source of the centrality measure.
Cohen and Malloy (2014), American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 'Friends in High Places'. Alumni-network basis for Senate voting; motivates the alumni network.
Qu and Lee (2015), Journal of Econometrics: SAR model with endogenous spatial weight matrix. Source of the control-function correction.
Anselin (1988), Geographical Analysis: LM diagnostics for spatial dependence. Basis for ML estimation of the SAR model.
Arnold, Deen and Patterson (2000), State and Local Government Review: friendship and votes; committee membership predicts friendship.
Caldeira, Clark and Patterson (1993), Legislative Studies Quarterly: political respect; shared committee assignments predict friendship.
Masket (2008), Quarterly Journal of Political Science: seating proximity and cue-taking; shared committees and agreement.
Bratton and Rouse (2011), Legislative Studies Quarterly: committee sharing and cosponsorship.
Fowler (2006), Political Analysis: cosponsorship networks in Congress.
Cho and Fowler (2010), Journal of Politics: legislative success in a small world.
Canen and Trebbi (2016), mimeo: endogenous network formation in Congress; structural model of voting with social ties.
Dekel, Jackson and Wolinsky (2009), Quarterly Journal of Political Science: vote buying in legislatures and lobbying; theoretical base for contribution-game framing.
Bertrand, Bombardini and Trebbi (2014), American Economic Review: whom you know vs what you know in lobbying.
Romer and Snyder (1994) and Grier and Munger (1991): empirical PAC allocation, margin of victory and committee effects (control-variable sources).

rel.summary_md:
Battaglini and Patacchini model two opposed interest groups that bid for votes from legislators who care about money and about voting the same way as their peers. They prove the game has a unique equilibrium. When legislators are office-motivated and have log utility, each group pays each legislator in proportion to that legislator's Bonacich (Katz-Bonacich) centrality. When legislators also care about policy, the weights become a modified Bonacich centrality that depends on preferences and pivot probabilities, and it converges back to plain Bonacich in large chambers. The empirical part fits a spatial-autoregressive model of total PAC money to U.S. House members across the 2004-2012 cycles. Ties come from shared committees (N=2,128 member-Congress rows, phi=0.209, 0.217 after a control-function correction) and shared alma maters (N=1,166, phi=0.084). Degree, closeness and betweenness explain nothing: R^2 stays at 0.148, the same as the model with no network terms. The authors chose not to build the network from cosponsorship, because cosponsorship is itself driven by money (fn. 30). This is an NBER working paper and has not been peer-reviewed.

The most direct bearing is on `fec/engine/kb_benchmark.py`, which cites this paper and implements its prediction as a diagnostic. Its design departs from the paper in three ways:
- It runs Katz on the cosponsorship-based kernel `build_P`, the network the paper avoids because cosponsorship depends on money.
- It pools the Senate with the House, while the paper covers the House only.
- It sets attenuation at 0.85 of the convergence bound, where the paper estimates a weaker spillover of about 0.08 to 0.25.

The stored results (Spearman rho 0.135 against CU money and 0.230 against bank plus financial-services money, n=533 across both chambers, file written 2026-08-18) are therefore unstratified, unverified, and about seven weeks stale. The paper also offers modest support, on a money outcome only, for keeping the degree/betweenness InfluenceScore out of the rank. It also points to a gap: in the allocator, money to one member reaches that member's network neighbours only after a discrete conversion.

bearings.paper_claim: In equilibrium, transfers are a monotonically increasing function of Bonacich centrality b=(I-beta*G)^-1*1. They are exactly proportional to it only when legislators are office-motivated and utility is logarithmic (Prop 1). Policy-motivated legislators get modified Bonacich weights that depend on preferences and pivot probabilities (eq. 15, Prop 2). Those converge to plain Bonacich as n grows (Prop 3). The estimated network-externality parameter is phi=0.2088 (SE 0.0697) on the committee network, 0.2165 after correction, and 0.0837 (SE 0.0262) on the alumni network.
bearings.system_side: A diagnostic outside the chain. It computes Katz-Bonacich on the live kernel build_P using out-walks, with delta = KB_DELTA 0.85 / spectral radius (stored: radius 1.502, delta 0.566). It then reports Spearman rho against the optimizer allocation, observed CU money, bank plus financial-services money, and the legislative score. The docstring says groups allocate 'IN PROPORTION TO' KB centrality. The member desk shows kb_pct taken from this file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper only derives the proportional form under office motivation and log utility. Under policy motivation the weights also depend on preferences and pivot probabilities, so the docstring overstates the claim. Whether 0.85 x (1/lambda_max) is comparable to phi of about 0.08-0.25 depends on the paper's W being row-normalized. The garbled text layer does not confirm that, so the comparison is suggestive, not exact. If W is row-normalized, the paper implies much shorter effective walks than the benchmark uses. The paper does not specify edge direction for this system's directed kernel, because its empirical networks are undirected.

bearings.paper_claim: The empirical test uses exogenous-leaning ties: shared committees with a Qu-Lee control-function correction, and shared alma maters. It deliberately does not use cosponsorship as the network, because cosponsorship is an endogenous outcome of contributions (fn. 30). The sample is House members only, 109th-113th Congresses. The outcome is total PAC money in logs, with controls for margin of victory (-0.897), DW-NOMINATE (-1.077), chair (+0.401), party, seniority and income.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.2.1 and fn. 30; Sec 4.2.2; Sec 4.3 Table 2-3 (p.21-26)
bearings.system_side: KB is computed on build_P over the cosponsorship network (MBC.load_network), which includes receiver-susceptibility edge_mult. All 533 members of both chambers are pooled. Seven of the 15 top-decile unallocated members are senators (for example Kennedy, Merkley, Warren, Scott, Cruz, Gillibrand). The correlations are raw Spearman with no controls. The stored rho values (kb_benchmark.json, written 2026-08-18) are: optimizer allocation 0.247 (n=533), CU money 0.135 (n=533), bank plus financial-services money 0.230 (n=533), legislative score 0.654 (n=533).
bearings.transfer_conditions: A KB-versus-money correlation on a cosponsorship graph cannot test the B-P equilibrium. Money may drive cosponsorship, so the reverse-causation path the paper designed around is open here. Chamber and party are both known fault lines, and the paper has no Senate evidence. The benchmark's rho values must carry an UNSTRATIFIED label and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path, stratified by chamber with B-P-style controls, reproduces them. The paper's outcome is aggregate PAC money in the 2004-2012 cycles; the system uses a single industry's money in the current window, so magnitudes do not transfer.

bearings.paper_claim: Degree, closeness and betweenness centrality do not explain PAC contributions. Committee degree is 0.0004 (SE 0.0003), alumni degree -0.0018 (SE 0.0053), closeness 0.590 (SE 0.471), and betweenness -4.9e-05 (SE 2.9e-05). R^2 is 0.148 in every Table 4 specification, the same as the no-network baseline. Only the Bonacich-type SAR term carries signal (LR 11.13 committee, 9.62 alumni).
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore = 0.60 normalized weighted out-degree + 0.25 betweenness + 0.15 eigenvector. It has been retired from the Influence pillar (AB13 = 0) as direction-blind, but it still feeds the underdog lens's Intrinsic composite.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's outcome is PAC money received, not influence or bill passage. It supports keeping degree- and betweenness-heavy scores out of any money-allocation or money-predicting role, and is neutral on whether they measure legislative influence. The evidence comes from House committee and alumni networks in 2004-2012, not cosponsorship networks. It indirectly questions the underdog lens, which still treats this composite as intrinsic influence.

bearings.paper_claim: Because legislators value voting the same way as their peers, a group pricing a legislator counts the downstream effect through all network walks (the Bonacich multiplier), not only the legislator's own vote. The estimated externality is phi of about 0.21 (committee) and 0.08 (alumni), both positive and significant.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 2 (conformity utility); Sec 3.2.1 Prop 1; Sec 4.3 Table 2
bearings.system_side: pflip combines a money term with a one-hop peer term nA/mAt, where nA counts only neighbours already in the discrete 'pro' camp. A CU dollar to member m raises only m's own pflip. Neighbours' pflip changes only after m crosses a defection threshold and is converted, which clears the cache and recomputes proximity.
bearings.transfer_conditions: phi measures network autocorrelation in contributions received, and could reflect correlated effects rather than vote conformity. The paper does not show that money to one member moves a peer's vote. Any continuous spillover term would be a new modeling choice that needs its own pre-registered look, not a calibration taken from this paper. The theory is a two-sided equilibrium, while the system's optimizer allocates for one PAC, so the transfer is conceptual only.

gaps_exposed: No exogenous social-tie layer. Every diffusion and centrality kernel is built from cosponsorship, which the paper treats as endogenous to money (fn. 30). There is no shared-committee co-membership network and no alumni network, although the paper shows both carry a significant externality (phi 0.209 committee, 0.084 alumni).

The KB attenuation (KB_DELTA 0.85 in kb_benchmark.py; attenuation_fraction 0.82 in the dashboard template) is set near the convergence bound, not estimated. Nothing estimates a network-externality parameter with a likelihood-ratio test against a no-network baseline, as the paper's SAR maximum-likelihood fit does.

The benchmark is raw Spearman with no controls. The paper shows margin of victory, DW-NOMINATE, chair, party and seniority are large predictors of PAC money, so an uncontrolled rho mixes centrality with these covariates.
kb_benchmark pools both chambers and is not stratified by chamber or party. The paper's evidence is House-only.
In the joint optimizer, money spills over to peers only through discrete conversions, with no continuous network multiplier on the value of a dollar.
data/network/kb_benchmark.json was last written 2026-08-18, despite a weekly-refresh step at fec/weekly_refresh.py:523. The member desk still shows kb_pct from this stale file.
flags: UNSTRATIFIED: kb_benchmark.json correlations (rho 0.135 vs CU money, 0.230 vs bank plus financial-services money, 0.247 vs optimizer allocation; n=533 House+Senate; written 2026-08-18; money window = whatever congestion.json held then, cycle not recorded) pool across chamber and party, both known fault lines. Quote them only with that label.

UNVERIFIED (DE-062): no second path has reproduced the KB-versus-money rho values. They also come from the cosponsorship network, which this paper deliberately avoids as endogenous to contributions, so they cannot be presented as a test of the Battaglini-Patacchini equilibrium.

The kb_benchmark.py docstring (lines 2-5) says groups allocate 'IN PROPORTION TO KATZ-BONACICH CENTRALITY'. The paper gives exact proportionality only for office-motivated legislators with log utility; otherwise the weights are modified Bonacich or monotone functions.

D-025 wording check: the dashboard tooltip and member row say 'Reach on this issue: top X% of Congress', computed from Katz on the PE kernel (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:523,1032). This is a heuristic model output. The paper supports Katz-Bonacich only as an equilibrium money-pricing benchmark, never as reach, access or closeness. This is borderline and is not a confirmed violation.
The stale artifact (2026-08-18) predates COMPET_MULT default-on (2026-10-06) and the later kernel and receptivity changes, so the desk's kb_pct is out of date.

Internal inconsistencies in the source: the text says LR p = 0.000, but Table 3 brackets show 0.003 (committee) and 0.001 (alumni). The introduction says 'business PAC contributions' while Sec 4.2.2 uses total PAC money. It is an NBER working paper, not peer-reviewed.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization), so neither is in conflict.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul listed Battaglini and Patacchini twice in his Social Network Analysis bibliography with no annotation text, so there is no takeaway for the evidence to contradict and nothing has gone stale. The system has already gone further than his notes: kb_benchmark.py is built directly from this paper. That design choice fits his highlight of Ardekani's preference for Katz over PageRank and closeness, and his view that forms of centrality need more research. Table 4, where degree, closeness and betweenness explain no PAC money, is consistent with the system retiring direction-blind centrality, which his Sotoudeh highlights also support. What his record does not yet capture is the paper's own caution: the authors refuse to use cosponsorship as the network. Paul plans to build his social network analysis on cosponsorship, and the benchmark does the same. A note recording that the benchmark is a cosponsorship-graph, two-chamber, uncontrolled approximation of the paper's test would bring his record up to date.

related.why: Paul highlighted Ardekani's choice of Katz prestige over PageRank and closeness. Battaglini and Patacchini supply the equilibrium reason why Katz-Bonacich, not degree, closeness or betweenness, should price legislators.
Porter et al. build the committee co-membership network of the House. B-P use exactly this kind of shared-committee tie as their main network, which the system lacks as a layer.

Sotoudeh et al. find cosponsorship centrality is a weak indicator of bill passage. B-P find that standard centralities do not explain PAC money and avoid cosponsorship networks as endogenous. Together they caution against cosponsorship centrality as a stand-in for either influence or money value.
Ringe et al. propose co-voting network centrality as a measure of influence. B-P give a money-allocation equilibrium for which centrality family should matter.

Both papers model competing budgeted actors who allocate resources across networked voters. Romero Moreno's shadowing and shielding heuristics are the dynamic counterpart to B-P's static Bonacich-weighted equilibrium.
Bonica models how PACs allocate contributions by ideology and competitiveness. B-P add network position as a separate determinant and control for DW-NOMINATE and margin of victory.
